3.5 — Player Projectile: Clone, Retag & Reuse the Cooldown

The turret has been shooting you since 3.2. Time to shoot back. None of today's code is really new — the bullet is a clone, the trigger was already on it, and the rate limit is the timer you built in 3.3. What is new is that a bullet cannot aim itself, so the player has to tell it where to go.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I let the player shoot back?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

The turret already shoots. The player should shoot back, and almost none of that is new code: the bullet is the turret's bullet with a different tag and a different colour, the trigger is the trigger it already had, and the rate limit is the timer from 3.3. What is genuinely new is that the bullet cannot aim itself — it has to be told, at the instant it is born, which way it is going.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Clone the enemy bullet instead of writing a second oneRight-click Turret_Projectile in the Project window and duplicate it. A bullet is a sprite, a trigger and a script; you already built all three, and the second one is a copy.Read: the prefab you assembled in 3.2.
  2. Change the two things that make it yoursRename it Player_Projectile, set its tag to Fireball — the enemy bullet is E_Fireball, and the tag is the only thing that will ever tell the two apart — and recolour the sprite so a human can tell them apart too.Read: the tag-versus-type discussion in 3.4.
  3. Give the new script a direction and a lifespanVector3 direction; and float lifespan = 2;. A direction is not a speed — it is a unit vector saying which way, multiplied by speed on the frame it moves.Read: the Vector3 and Time.deltaTime rows of the quick reference.
  4. Turn a facing into a directionSetDirection(String facing) compares the string your player already stores against "Right", "Left", "Up" and "Down" and assigns the matching unit Vector3. Four branches, no maths.Read: the facing block you wrote in 1.6.
  5. write this partRead: the Instantiate() row from 3.2 and the timer from 3.3.

Four of the five parts are a copy of work you have already done — and that is the lesson. The one part with no precedent is the hand-off: the object is created by one script and configured by it in the same breath, before the first Update() ever runs.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the player shoot" cannot be looked up. "Tell a newly created object which way to move" can — it is one method call on the result of Instantiate().

Your turn

The bullet is cloned from the turret's and told its direction by a string. Name one thing that would break if you later added a fifth facing, like "UpRight" — and say where the fix would go.

Nothing in this project reacts to the Fireball tag yet, so your bullet currently passes through every enemy in the game. Is that a bug, or a feature that is one lesson away from working?

In the Editor ~20 min
  1. Project window → Assets/Prefabs, right-click Turret_Projectile → Duplicate, and rename the copy Player_Projectile. You are copying a prefab that already works.
  2. Inspector → Player_Projectile → Tag: set it to Fireball. The turret's bullet is E_Fireball, and that tag is the only thing that will ever tell the two apart. If Fireball is not in the list, add it in Tags and Layers first.
  3. Inspector → Sprite Renderer → Color: tint it. A bullet the player cannot tell from the enemy's is a bullet the player will run into.
  4. Project window → Assets/Scripts → right-click → Create → C# Script → PlayerProjectile. Note the name matches the class inside it — Unity requires that, and a mismatch stops the script from attaching.
  5. Inspector → Player_Projectile → Add Component → Player Projectile, then remove the old Projectile component. One bullet, one script. Two scripts both moving the same object is a bug that looks like a framerate problem.
  6. Hierarchy → select Player → Inspector → Player Controller. Because the Player in a scene is a prefab instance, an empty Projectile slot here is an override — click Overrides → Apply All after you wire it, or the next Player you place will be missing it.
In the Code ~20 min
APIWhat it gives youWhat it costs
Instantiate(prefab, position, Quaternion.identity) A live copy of the prefab, and the copy itself back as a return value so you can configure it. Every copy is a new object in the scene — nothing cleans them up for you.
GetComponent<PlayerProjectile>() The component on the object at the other end of the reference. It returns null if the object has no such component — and then throws on the next dot.
Vector3 direction * speed * Time.deltaTime A movement step that is frame-independent and points anywhere you like. A direction that is not unit length quietly changes the speed.
CompareTag("Fireball") The cheapest way for something else to know what hit it. Nothing on the other side has it yet — the tag only starts working when a receiver asks.
The tag is doing nothing yet, and that is on purpose. Nothing in this project reacts to Fireball today, so your bullet passes through every enemy in the game. It is not broken — it is waiting for a receiver. The enemy that flinches when it is hit arrives in Unit 4, and the tag you set today is the handle it will grab.

Socratic: Whose Job Is Aiming?

  1. The turret's bullet seeks a target it was handed; the player's bullet moves in a direction it was told. Both were written by you. Which model is better for a weapon the player aims — and what does the turret's version get that yours cannot?
  2. SetDirection takes a String. What would you have to change if the player could face eight directions instead of four, and where would that change have to happen?
  3. Your bullet and the turret's are two nearly identical files. What is the argument for keeping them separate, and what is the argument for one script with a flag?
In the CodeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I let the player shoot back?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerProjectile.cs. A new script on the cloned prefab, and one new method on the player. The bullet moves itself; the player only decides the direction and pays the cooldown. One line is left for you — the hand-off.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Store what the bullet needs to know

Three fields at the top of a brand-new PlayerProjectile script. Two of them you have written before.

    float speed = 10;
    Vector3 direction;
    float lifespan = 2;
  1. 1Faster than the turret's 8, because a player who has to line up a shot should be rewarded for it. A plain field, not serialized — no designer is going to tune a bullet mid-fight.
  2. 2Which way it is going, as a unit vector: (1,0,0) right, (-1,0,0) left, and so on. It starts as zero and stays zero until somebody sets it — which is what the blank line below is about.
  3. 3The cleanup from 3.2, shortened. A player bullet that misses should disappear before it can cross the whole level.

Step 2Move it, and destroy it when its time is up

The same two jobs as Projectile.cs, in the same order — but this bullet has no target to seek, so the movement is one line of arithmetic instead of a MoveTowards call.

    void Update()
    {
        lifespan -= Time.deltaTime;
        if (lifespan < 0)
        {
            Destroy(gameObject);
        }

        transform.position += direction * speed * Time.deltaTime;
    }
  1. 3Count down using deltaTime, exactly as 3.3 taught you: subtracting a per-frame constant would make the bullet live longer on a faster machine.
  2. 4When the timer runs out, the bullet removes itself. Note < 0 and not <= 0: it does not matter here, and matching the file you already wrote matters more than shaving a frame.
  3. 6gameObject is the bullet — the object this component sits on.
  4. 9The movement. A unit direction times a speed times a frame time, added to where the bullet already is. This is transform movement, not a body — the same choice the turret bullet made, and it is fine here because nothing in this project collides with a bullet.

Step 3Turn a facing into a direction

SetDirection is public because the player calls it from a different object, and it takes the same four strings the animation code already uses.

    public void SetDirection(String facing)
    {
        if (facing == "Right")
        {
            direction = new Vector3(1, 0, 0);
        }
        else if (facing == "Left")
        {
            direction = new Vector3(-1, 0, 0);
        }
        else if (facing == "Up")
        {
            direction = new Vector3(0, 1, 0);
        }
        else if (facing == "Down")
        {
            direction = new Vector3(0, -1, 0);
        }
    }
  1. 1String (capital S) is the System type — the same using System; at the top of your player file. Its parameter is the word your facing field holds.
  2. 3Four independent branches, one per direction. Compare a string with == in C# and you get a value comparison, not a check that they are the same object — which is the behaviour you want and not what some other languages give you.
  3. 5Right is positive X. Unit length on purpose — (1,0,0) is one unit long, so multiplying by speed gives exactly speed. Writing new Vector3(5, 0, 0) here would silently make the bullet five times faster.
  4. 9The same length in the opposite direction.
  5. 19There is no else. If facing is ever null or something unexpected, direction stays (0,0,0) and the bullet sits where it spawned until the lifespan deletes it. Watch for that if you ever rename a facing string.

Step 4Spawn it, and tell it which way — this is the blank

Back in PlayerController. The prefab is in the Inspector slot; the spawn and the hand-off are two lines.

    [SerializeField] GameObject projectile;

    void Shoot()
    {
        GameObject playerProjectileCopy = Instantiate(projectile, transform.position, Quaternion.identity);
________________
    }

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) && cooldownTimer < 0)
        {
            Shoot();
            cooldownTimer = .5f;
        }
  1. 1The slot, wired in the Prefab overrides on your Player. A GameObject, not a component, because Instantiate() needs the whole object to copy.
  2. 5Three arguments, same three as the turret. What to copy, where to put it — here transform.position, the player's own centre — and what rotation. Quaternion.identity is "no rotation", and Instantiate() hands you back the copy so you can talk to it.
  3. Your turn6The hand-off, and the whole new idea in this lesson. You have a copy of the prefab and a facing string. Reach into the copy, get its PlayerProjectile component, and call SetDirection(facing). Two method calls with a dot between them; no new, no loop.
  4. 9The trigger, inside Update(). cooldownTimer is the field from 3.3 that counts down every frame; < 0 means "the weapon is ready". It is shared with the melee swing, so shooting and swinging take turns — one timer, two weapons.
  5. 12Reset after firing, not before. The same order as 3.3: act, then arm the next one.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Three things to check: the tag on the clones is Fireball and the turret's is still E_Fireball; the projectile slot on your Player is filled in the Prefab overrides, not left empty; and SetDirection is called on the copy, not on the prefab. A bullet with no direction does not error — it just sits there, which is much harder to diagnose.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerProjectile.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using System;
using UnityEngine;

// PlayerProjectile.cs - a bullet that knows where it is going because the
// player told it, once, at the moment it spawned.
public class PlayerProjectile : MonoBehaviour
{
    float speed = 10;
    Vector3 direction;
    float lifespan = 2;

    void Update()
    {
        lifespan -= Time.deltaTime;
        if (lifespan < 0)
        {
            Destroy(gameObject);
        }

        transform.position += direction * speed * Time.deltaTime;
    }

    public void SetDirection(String facing)
    {
        if (facing == "Right")
        {
            direction = new Vector3(1, 0, 0);
        }
        else if (facing == "Left")
        {
            direction = new Vector3(-1, 0, 0);
        }
        else if (facing == "Up")
        {
            direction = new Vector3(0, 1, 0);
        }
        else if (facing == "Down")
        {
            direction = new Vector3(0, -1, 0);
        }
    }
}

// PlayerController.cs - the half that spawns and aims it:
//   [SerializeField] GameObject projectile;
//
//   void Shoot()
//   {
//       GameObject playerProjectileCopy =
//           Instantiate(projectile, transform.position, Quaternion.identity);
//       playerProjectileCopy.GetComponent<PlayerProjectile>().SetDirection(facing);
//   }
Build Lab: Shoot It ~15 min

Play, and check four things in this order. If number one fails, the rest cannot work.

CheckWhat it proves
Press Space four times quicklyExactly one bullet appears every half second. The 3.3 timer is doing its job for a second weapon.
Face each direction and fireThe bullet leaves in the right one. If it always goes right, facing was never set before Shoot() ran.
Fire and waitThe bullet disappears after about two seconds instead of living forever.
Fire at a turretNothing happens. The tag has no receiver yet — see the callout above.
An empty projectile slot throws on the first Space press, not at startup. Instantiate(null, ...) is an error that only appears the first time you shoot, so it is easy to test everything else and assume the file is fine. Wire the slot, then apply the override.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why the player's bullet is a clone with a different tag rather than a new prefab
  • Say what a unit direction is, and what happens if it is not unit length
  • Configure an object you just created, in the same method that created it
  • Say which tag on which prefab belongs to which side, without opening the project
  • Commit and push
